title: Elin and the Cosmic Shadow
markdown:
Dawn crackled. Sunlight burst through Elin’s window. She practically bounced out of bed, a science whiz with a mission from Dr. Ada Brook: become a starlight detective. Spot tiny blinks in distant stars’ light — signals that might mean unseen worlds zipping past.

“Patience,” Brook had said. “The universe whispers.”

Whispers. Elin craved a roar. She dashed to the observation pool. Bramble, a seal pup with pebble-sparkling eyes, barked hello and nudged a bright red ball. Splash. The ball bobbed, then bumped the water’s edge. A tiny ripple spread, distorting the brilliant lab lights on the surface. The reflection flickered, turning fuzzy.

Elin stopped. Brow furrowed. The ball, the water, the distorted light — it changed the reflection. Made the shining lights look dimmer. Bramble nudged again. Another splash. Another ripple. Another fuzzy flicker.

“Wait.” A jolt. A new idea clicked. “Bramble, you water-wiggling genius.”

She sprinted to the telescope console, leaving wet footprints that Brook would later call data contamination and then forgive. Heart thumping. Brook’s words, revised: the dips in starlight were not ‘no light.’ They were an interruption. A shadow. Like the ball blocking the reflection and making it dimmer. The pool still shivered. The lab lights still lied about being steady.

“A shadow,” she said, voice cracking. Fingers a blur on the console, hunting that same dimming. “Something passed in front of the star. Just like your ball. A tiny dip in the light.”

Bramble barked, thrilled. “My splashes are world-changing.”

Trembling, she focused on a distant star Brook had starred on the list as maybe, don’t get attached. Data streamed. Filters adjusted for the tell-tale pattern, the flicker. The first dip might have been a truck on the coast road; she waited. Then — there. A tiny dip on the graph. Then another, same depth, same width, like a polite knock repeating. A consistent, rhythmic blink. Not a cloud. Not a sneeze on the lens. Periodicity. A new world, or at least a candidate that would survive Brook’s scepticism and Bramble’s next splash.

Brook padded in. “Any luck? Did it whisper?”

Elin pointed at the screen, grin triumphant. “A dance. Something waltzing in front of its star.”

Brook peered. A radiant smile. “You saw the pattern. The ball showed how a passing object dims the light. That is how we find planets. Transits. Not magic. Geometry and patience.”

Elin gazed at the blinking graph. She did not ask what other secrets hid in the light. She exported the dip file, labelled it bramble-period, and tossed the red ball back so the seal could run the demonstration for the next intern, who would almost certainly get wet. Brook put the kettle on. The star, unimpressed, dimmed on schedule. Elin counted the next dip aloud, just to hear it be ordinary and enormous at once, a whisper that had finally agreed to be a number.
